EXPLAINER from the 15 councillors who oppose turning Toronto Water into a utility: how your water system is paid for today, and what to ask before Monday.

1/ Toronto Water is a City division. It is publicly owned and run, and it answers to Council.

2/ It is rate-supported. Water and wastewater rates pay for it, not property taxes. Council sets those rates every year in public, as part of the rate-supported budget.

3/ The needs are real. Aging watermains, basement flooding protection, lead service line replacement, climate resilience and Lake Ontario water quality all call for steady, long-term capital investment. On that, we agree with supporters of the utility proposal.

4/ Our view is that the current public structure can meet those needs. Council can use dedicated reserves, binding multi-year capital plans, firm rules to keep water revenue for water, and stronger federal and provincial funding. A new board and new borrowing arrangements aren't needed, and rate decisions don't have to move further from residents.

5/ Ask candidates in your ward and for mayor:
- Who would set water rates, and would those votes happen in public at Council?
- What legal limits would stop a future sale, contracting out or P3s?
- How would any new borrowing affect your bill?
- What would happen to basement flooding and lead pipe programs during a transition?

6/ No change to Toronto Water's governance can happen without a vote of Council. We will keep raising these questions there, whoever wins on October 26.

We do not endorse any mayoral candidate. Public water, public accountability. Polls are open Monday, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Find your voting place at toronto.ca/elections or call 311.

STATEMENT from the 15 councillors who oppose turning Toronto Water into a stand-alone utility, responding to Councillor Bradford's written commitment.

We welcome Councillor Bradford's statement, as reported by the Globe, that Toronto Water will stay 100% publicly owned and will not be sold or privatized. Residents asked for that commitment in writing. We thank our colleague for providing it, and we take him at his word.

A commitment made during a campaign is a good first step. The safeguards that last a generation are the ones written into binding rules, and four questions are still open:

1. Contracting out and P3s. The statement does not cover these. Will operations, maintenance or new capital projects be protected from contracting out and P3 arrangements, in law or bylaw?
2. Rate-setting. Will Council keep approving water and wastewater rates every year, in public, or would a utility board set them?
3. Borrowing. Would the utility borrow on its own account? If so, how would debt costs show up on ratepayers' bills?
4. Oversight. What reports would the utility make to Council, and could a future Council reverse the change?

Our view hasn't changed. The capital backlog is real: watermains, basement flooding protection, lead service lines and climate resilience. It can be addressed inside the current public structure, through dedicated reserves, binding multi-year capital plans and fair funding from the federal and provincial governments.

No change to how Toronto Water is governed can happen without a vote of Council. Whoever wins on Monday, we will ask for these answers in writing before any such vote. We do not endorse a mayoral candidate.

comments.name: Liaison Strategies
comments.content:
A methodology note on the "60% worried about privatization" figure, without taking a side on the policy. Credit to the councillors for disclosing that the water workers' union commissioned it.

A poll paid for by an interested party isn't automatically wrong. But before treating any single number as settled, readers should check four things:
1) The exact question wording. "Worried about privatization of city services" measures general concern. It isn't a test of support for or opposition to a specific utility proposal.
2) The question order. Questions asked earlier in a survey can prime how people answer later ones.
3) The field dates, sample size, method and margin of error.
4) Whether the full tables are public.

Generic concern about privatization tends to poll high. Reaction to a specific governance model, once people hear the details, is a separate thing to measure.

This applies to every sponsor on every side, including our own clients. That's why we publish wording and full tables. Treat it as a snapshot, and give more weight to the trend and to multiple independent sources.
